nameStory: The sawtooth oak gets its name from the distinctive sharp, pointed teeth along the edges of its leaves that look just like the jagged edge of a saw blade. Each leaf margin is lined with these bristle-tipped teeth that feel prickly to the touch, making this one of the easiest oaks to identify by name alone.
description: Sawtooth oak is a medium to large deciduous tree from Asia that can grow 40-60 feet tall with a broad, rounded crown. Unlike most of our native New England oaks with their lobed leaves, this species has simple, unlobed leaves that are long and narrow with very distinctive saw-toothed edges. It's an introduced species that's occasionally planted as an ornamental and has escaped cultivation in some areas, though it remains quite rare in New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow leaves (4-8 inches) with sharp, bristle-tipped teeth along the entire edge - no lobes like typical oaks. The leaves feel somewhat thick and leathery, with prominent parallel veins running from the midrib to each tooth point.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are surrounded by distinctive soft, silky bristles that feel fuzzy to the touch - quite different from the smooth, hard buds of most native oaks.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Acorns are small and oval, about 3/4 inch long, sitting in cups covered with long, curly, almost hair-like scales that feel soft and bristly. The acorns take two years to mature.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature bark is dark gray to brown with deep furrows and ridges, similar to other oaks but often with a slightly more plated appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a medium to large tree with a broad, somewhat rounded crown. Young trees often have a more pyramidal shape that becomes rounder with age.

habitat: In New England, sawtooth oak is mainly found in cultivated settings like parks, arboretums, and large residential properties where it was planted as an ornamental. It occasionally escapes cultivation and may be found along woodland edges, disturbed areas, or near developed land. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring with a fresh yellow-green color. Small, inconspicuous flowers appear as dangling catkins (male) and tiny clusters (female) in May.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive sawtooth leaves are at their most prominent, deep green and fully expanded, making identification easiest during this season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to golden-brown in autumn, and mature acorns drop from their bristly cups. Fall color is usually not as spectacular as native oaks.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the characteristic fuzzy, bristle-surrounded buds that are diagnostic of this species. Some small acorn cups may persist on branches.

funFact: This oak is sometimes called the 'wildlife magnet' because its acorns are incredibly attractive to deer, squirrels, and turkeys - so much so that wildlife managers specifically plant it to create feeding areas, even though a single tree can produce over 1,000 pounds of acorns in a good year!
confusionNotes: The sawtooth-edged, unlobed leaves make this nearly impossible to confuse with any native New England oak, which all have distinctly lobed leaves. It might be confused with chestnut trees at first glance, but chestnuts have much larger, coarser teeth and completely different bark and buds.
contextualKnowledge: Many people are surprised to learn this is actually an oak since it looks so different from our familiar lobed-leaf native oaks. It belongs to a section of oaks found mainly in Asia and parts of Europe that have toothed rather than lobed leaves. Despite being non-native, it's generally not considered invasive in New England due to its rarity.
compareHints: Sawtooth oak is completely different from all other New England oaks because of its simple, toothed leaves rather than the lobed leaves found on species like white oak, red oak, or black oak. The fuzzy winter buds and bristly acorn cups also set it apart from native species. Among oaks, only the closely related Turkey oak shares these characteristics, but Turkey oak has somewhat lobed leaves rather than the simple toothed leaves of sawtooth oak.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England oaks, white oak is distinguished by its evenly rounded leaf lobes without bristle tips (unlike red oak group species) and its light gray bark.

Among New England's oaks, northern red oak is distinguished by its pointed leaf lobes (white oak has rounded lobes), its large size (much bigger than bear oak or dwarf chinkapin oak), and its relatively shallow acorn caps (deeper than scarlet oak, shallower than pin oak).
Bear oak stands apart from other New England oaks by being consistently shrubby rather than tree-like, even at maturity.
Among the red oak group, black oak has the deepest leaf lobes - much deeper than red oak or pin oak.
Unlike white oak with its deeply rounded lobes, chestnut oak has scalloped edges with rounded teeth.
Among New England's white oak group, swamp white oak is unique in its preference for wet areas and its distinctive leaf shape with deeper bottom lobes.
Among New England's red oaks, scarlet oak stands out with its deeply dissected leaves that have the most pronounced sinuses (indentations).
Unlike other New England oaks that have lobed leaves (deeply indented edges), dwarf chinkapin oak has simple leaves with rounded teeth like a saw blade.
English oak stands out among New England's oaks by having the leaf and acorn stems completely reversed from most natives - very short leaf stems but very long acorn stems.
Among New England oaks, pin oak stands out for its combination of deeply-cut leaves with sharp points and its distinctive pin-like branching pattern.
Among New England oaks, bur oak is easily distinguished by its enormous acorns with fringed caps and extremely deeply-lobed leaves.
Among New England oaks, post oak is unique for its cross-shaped leaves with rounded lobes and fuzzy undersides.
Unlike most New England oaks, chinkapin oak has toothed rather than lobed leaves, setting it apart immediately from white oak, red oak, and others.
Unlike our native oaks, Turkey oak has those telltale bristly buds and bristle-tipped leaves that you can actually feel.
Among New England oaks, willow oak is unmistakable due to its unlobed, willow-like leaves - all other regional oaks have distinctly lobed or toothed leaves.
Among New England oaks, shingle oak is instantly recognizable by its simple, unlobed leaves - all other common oaks in the region have the typical lobed leaves we associate with oaks.
